newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy to include "Europe tax" in 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy to include "Europe tax" in 1997 budget.

text.p: Italy's government said on Thursday it had drawn up a 1997 budget that would include a special "Euro-tax" to help slash the deficit and put the country on course to join Europe's planned single currency.

Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi said the measures in the package aimed to cut next year's deficit by a hefty 50 trillion lire ($32.8 billion), well in excess of the previously expected 32.4 trillion.

He told reporters after a summit of coalition party leaders chaired by Prime Minister Romano Prodi that it would include cuts of two trillion lire in health spending and the same off pensions as well as the extraordinary "Euro-tax".

He said the measures would help reduce the ratio of deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) to three percent in 1997, the magic figure countries must meet to make the grade for joining monetary union when it starts in 1999.
"The numbers to get into Europe are there and they will take us to three percent," Fantozzi said. "They will allow us to be with the other countries from the start."
The cabinet is due to approve the budget on Friday before submitting it to parliament, which must pass it into law by the end of December.
Prodi's government, appointed in May, relies for support in the lower house on the hard left Communist Refoundation party.

It had resisted pressure from the Treasury to cut spending on health and pensions but leader Fausto Bertinotti indicated after the summit with Prodi that the party may find the package palatable, saying he was confident it would be equitable.
"Even if there continue to be problems, we have made a significant step forward," Bertinotti told reporters.
Prodi's efforts to put together a budget stringent enough to keep alive Italy's hopes of joining a European currency union by the starting date of 1999 have gained increasing urgency in recent days.
The initial budget outlines foresaw a deficit to GDP ratio of only 4.5 percent, meaning Italy risked missing the boat.
Further pressure for a tougher-than-anticipated budget has come from evidence of a shortfall in 1996 accounts.
Details of the planned "Euro tax" have so far been vague.
A government source said the tax would raise between 10 trillion and 12 trillion lire in 1997.
Corriere della Sera newspaper on Thursday said it would be levied in the form of a once-off increase in income tax.
The planned extraordinary tax may receive a hostile reception in a country which already bears one of the heaviest tax burdens in Europe.
A Datamedia opinion poll conducted on Wednesday showed 56.4 percent of a sample of 1,002 Italians were not prepared to pay the tax.
